Let’s dive into Chapter 8—Ongoing Self-Assessment: Measuring and Tracking Emotional Intelligence Growth.
Think of emotional intelligence as a lifelong journey, not a finish line you cross once and forget about. Just like staying physically fit, keeping your EQ strong calls for regular check-ins and a willingness to adjust as you go.
So, how do you know if you’re making progress? It all starts with a little honest reflection. Take some time to look back at your recent interactions. Were there moments when you handled your emotions well? Or maybe a few situations where things could've gone better? This isn’t about judging yourself—it’s about seeing things clearly, so you can make smart choices moving forward.
There are some great, hands-on tools you can use for self-assessment. For instance, try journaling about your emotional experiences and the lessons you pick up along the way. Or, tap into your support network—ask a trusted friend, colleague, or mentor for their honest feedback about your emotional strengths and, yes, those blind spots we all have.
Another practical trick? Use self-rating scales. Every so often, rate yourself on the four core EQ domains: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management. It’s a simple way to track how you’re changing over time.
And don’t forget to set clear, specific goals. Maybe you decide to focus on listening more deeply this month or work on managing stress in a healthier way. That kind of focus really adds up.
Let me give you a real-world example. Suppose you’ve noticed you get impatient during team meetings. By journaling about those moments and asking for feedback, you might discover your impatience comes from a sense of urgency or frustration when things move slowly. With that insight, you can set a small goal: next time you feel that urge, pause and take a breath before responding. Over time, those little changes can turn into powerful new habits.
The key here is to approach self-assessment with curiosity and a bit of self-compassion. You’re not aiming for perfection—just progress. We all have emotional blind spots and slip-ups. What really matters is your willingness to learn and adapt.
When you make self-assessment a regular practice, you create a feedback loop that actually speeds up your growth. You’ll start noticing your emotional patterns sooner, you’ll adapt your strategies faster, and—maybe most importantly—you’ll have more reasons to celebrate your successes along the way.
